description: Curated real-world chronology for Impossible Timeline. Dates represent the earliest documented appearance, surviving attestation or public debut used by the game; episode facts are joined from episodes.json at runtime.

entries.event: World-bearing turtle imagery is attested in ancient South Asian cosmological traditions preserved in Sanskrit literature.
Spanish reports connected a Muisca investiture ritual involving gold offerings with the developing legend of El Dorado.
entries.source: Early Spanish accounts of the Muisca ritual

entries.event: The skaldic poem Eiríksmál describes the fallen ruler Erik Bloodaxe being welcomed into Odin's hall.
Horace evokes the Danaids' endless punishment of trying to fill a vessel that cannot retain water.
Pindar recounts Heracles' encounter with Augeas and the reward connected with cleansing the king's cattle domain.
Ovid links the broken horn of Achelous with the horn of plenty filled with fruit and flowers.
The Iliad describes Hephaestus working at his forge and crafting extraordinary armour for Achilles.
Plutarch records how Athenians preserved Theseus' ship by replacing decayed timbers, creating the celebrated identity paradox.
The Poetic Edda manuscript tradition preserves references to Gungnir, Odin's spear.
The surviving Poetic Edda manuscript tradition preserves Sleipnir as Odin's exceptional eight-legged horse.
A monumental palace built from ice was erected in Saint Petersburg during the reign of Empress Anna Ivanovna.
entries.source: Accounts of the Saint Petersburg Ice House

entries.event: Herodotus provides one of the earliest surviving Greek descriptions of the phoenix and its cycle of return.
Pindar's fourth Pythian Ode gives the earliest substantial surviving account of Jason's voyage for the Golden Fleece.
Writings associated with Zosimos of Panopolis document early alchemical ideas of transmutation that later developed into the philosopher's stone tradition.
Charles Perrault published Hop-o'-My-Thumb, whose ogre owns boots capable of crossing seven leagues at every stride.
entries.source: Charles Perrault, Histoires ou contes du temps passé

entries.event: Hesiod's Theogony names the Hydra of Lerna among the monstrous offspring faced by Heracles.
Hesiod places the Hesperides beyond Ocean and associates them with the guarded golden apples.
A Visit from St. Nicholas popularised Santa's airborne sleigh drawn by eight named reindeer.
Mikhail Lomonosov's Russian Grammar lists Baba Yaga among figures of Slavic popular belief, an early printed record of the character.
The Homeric Hymn to Hermes describes the young god's extraordinary movement and divine attributes.
Hesiod's Works and Days tells how Pandora opens a jar and releases afflictions into the human world.
The Poetic Edda manuscript tradition preserves Bifröst as the burning bridge between the human and divine realms.
Pindar's fourth Pythian Ode presents the Argo and its crew in the voyage undertaken by Jason.
The surviving Poetic Edda manuscript describes Yggdrasil as the immense ash at the centre of the Norse cosmos.
Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda recounts the forging of Draupnir and its power to reproduce eight rings every ninth night.
Jules Verne completed publication of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas, introducing Captain Nemo's electric submarine Nautilus.
entries.source: Jules Verne, Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

entries.event: Ovid's Metamorphoses preserves the celebrated version in which Midas receives the power to turn what he touches into gold.
Ovid gives the best-known surviving classical account of Daedalus and Icarus escaping with feather-and-wax wings.
The Odyssey describes Sisyphus in the underworld repeatedly forcing his immense stone uphill.
Apollonius of Rhodes' Argonautica presents Talos as the bronze guardian who circles Crete.
The Prose Edda recounts the forging of Thor's hammer Mjölnir and explains its unusually short handle.
Ovid's Metamorphoses relates how Daedalus built the labyrinth to conceal the Minotaur on Crete.
Plato introduced Atlantis in the dialogues Timaeus and Critias as a powerful island civilisation defeated and submerged.
The Odyssey refers to the wooden horse used by the Greeks to enter Troy, one of its earliest surviving literary attestations.
Geoffrey of Monmouth names Arthur's sword Caliburn in Historia Regum Britanniae, a direct ancestor of Excalibur.
entries.source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae

entries.event: The Tower of Babel narrative took its surviving written form in Genesis, reflecting the monumental temple towers of Mesopotamia.
John MacDonald's published travel narrative records sailors using the name Flying Dutchman for a phantom ship in stormy seas.
entries.source: John MacDonald, Travels in Various Parts of Europe, Asia and Africa

entries.event: The Homeric Hymn to Helios describes the sun god driving his chariot across the sky.
The developing Mahabharata tradition describes the Brahmastra among the divine weapons invoked by trained warriors.
Hesiod's Theogony recounts the birth of Pegasus from Medusa after she is slain by Perseus.
The TARDIS first appeared in An Unearthly Child, the opening episode of Doctor Who.
Doc Brown's DeLorean time machine debuted with the theatrical release of Back to the Future.
The Millennium Falcon entered popular culture with the original theatrical release of Star Wars.
UFO Robot Grendizer began its original Japanese television broadcast on Fuji TV.
